notes: Complete Commercial Court judgment on service out and forum non conveniens.

enrichment.short_title: Insurers' service out of jurisdiction set aside where Texas forum was more convenient
key_facts: Navigators and other underwriters sought declaratory relief that they had avoided or were not liable under an English-law project insurance policy covering a methanol plant in Equatorial Guinea.

Ampco and related defendants in Texas and the Cayman Islands disputed misrepresentation and non-disclosure over policy extensions said to conceal that commercial production had begun before substantial completion.
Leave to serve out in Texas and the Cayman Islands was granted in December 2002 and January 2003; defendants applied to set aside service.
Parallel proceedings in Oklahoma were dismissed on forum non conveniens grounds, but Harris County Texas proceedings were active with discovery and a trial date in March 2004.
The primary disputes were factual (plant completion status and production levels), with Texas witnesses and documents predominating.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court application to set aside an order permitting service of declaratory proceedings out of the jurisdiction.
enrichment.outcome: Application granted; service of the English proceedings set aside on forum non conveniens grounds, though the judge treated the insurers' arguable defence as borderline.
enrichment.ratio: Where service out is permitted under CPR 6.20 on an English-law insurance dispute, the court may still set aside service if England is not clearly the appropriate forum; a negative declaration of non-liability gives no special entitlement to an English trial where the centre of gravity of witnesses and parallel proceedings lies abroad.
legal_issues: Whether the claimants showed a serious issue to be tried on avoidance and coverage
Whether England was clearly the appropriate forum for trial
Whether concurrent proceedings in Texas justified setting aside service

notes: Complete VAT tribunal appeal on qualifying car input tax.

enrichment.short_title: Hotel company's VAT input tax denied on Rolls-Royce replacement not let at arm's length
key_facts: Crown & Cushion Hotel Ltd leased hotel inventory including a Rolls-Royce Silver Spirit to Eden Ltd for wedding use.
In 1998 the company replaced the unroadworthy Silver Spirit with a new Rolls-Royce Spur costing about £85,000 inclusive of VAT, without increasing rent.
HM Customs disallowed input tax recovery on the Spur purchase.

The tribunal found the replacement was not let for consideration equivalent to an arm's-length transaction and, applying Upton, that insurance covering private use meant intended availability for private use.
The Vice Chancellor upheld the tribunal on Article 7(2G)(a) but held the tribunal erred on Article 7(2G)(b) because the car was under Eden Ltd's exclusive control for business use.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal on points of law from a VAT and Duties Tribunal decision refusing input tax recovery.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; input tax credit remained disallowed because the non-arms-length letting ground was sufficient, despite partial success on the private-use point.
enrichment.ratio: Under Article 7(2G)(a) of the 1992 Order, input tax on a qualifying car is excluded where the letting consideration is less than that payable in a commercial arm's-length transaction, assessed by reference to transaction value rather than formal contractual structure alone.
legal_issues: Whether the Spur was let on hire for less than arm's-length consideration
Whether the purchaser intended to make the car available for private use under Article 7(2G)(b)
Whether the tribunal's findings were perverse or misdirected in law

notes: Full guidance judgment on UASC age assessment; post-judgment costs discussion included.

enrichment.short_title: Merton age assessment quashed for failure to put credibility concerns to asylum seeker
key_facts: The claimant, an unaccompanied asylum seeker from Ivory Coast, claimed to be aged 17 and sought accommodation under the Children Act 1989.
On 13 February 2003 Merton's social worker assessed him as at least 18, largely by appearance, demeanour and perceived inconsistencies in his account.
The decision letter stated the borough was taking the Home Office stance rather than giving adequate reasons.
A consultant paediatrician's report gave an age range of 18 plus or minus two years, consistent with either party's case.
Credibility concerns identified after the interview were not put to the claimant for explanation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of a local authority age assessment for an unaccompanied asylum-seeking child (UASC).
enrichment.outcome: Decision quashed; local authority directed to reconsider age on the material now available; claimant awarded costs.
enrichment.ratio: A local authority must make its own lawful age assessment rather than simply adopt the Home Office view, give adequate reasons, and afford procedural fairness by putting provisional adverse credibility findings to the applicant before deciding he is not a child.
legal_issues: What minimum standards govern lawful age assessment of young asylum seekers
Whether Merton made its own assessment or unlawfully adopted the Home Office decision
Whether the assessment process was procedurally fair
Whether medical evidence or verbatim notes were legally required

enrichment.short_title: Animal trade mark infringement succeeded against Animale despite limited partial revocation
key_facts: H Young (Animal brand) sued Medici for use of Animale on ladies' fashion goods.
Animal registered mark 2054886 covered broad classes including clothing; Animal sold surf-associated casual wear while Animale targeted older women.
Medici counterclaimed for partial revocation for non-use over the five-year period from April 1997 to April 2002.
The s.10(1) identical-mark claim was abandoned; infringement rested on likelihood of confusion under s.10(2).
Partial revocation narrowed some non-clothing specifications but clothing remained broadly protected.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court Chancery trial of trade mark infringement and passing off with a partial revocation counterclaim.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; counterclaim largely failed except limited narrowing of specifications in classes other than core clothing.
enrichment.ratio: Partial revocation depends on the fair description an average consumer would give to goods for which the mark has genuinely been used; use of Animal across mainstream casual clothing supported retaining 'clothing' rather than limiting the mark to surf-type wear for young purchasers.
legal_issues: Whether partial revocation should restrict Class 25 clothing to surf-type casual wear
What fair consumer description follows from the proprietor's actual use
Whether Animale was confusingly similar to Animal for clothing

notes: Complete appeal by case stated on Crown Court costs in firearms licensing appeal.

enrichment.short_title: Costs order against Chief Constable on firearms appeal quashed as Wednesbury unreasonable
key_facts: Mr Oldring, a shooting school proprietor, had shotgun and firearms certificates revoked after shooting a neighbour's cat.
He was later acquitted in the magistrates' court of criminal damage and causing unnecessary suffering.
On appeal the Crown Court restored his certificates and ordered the Chief Constable to pay his costs.
The Chief Constable appealed by case stated, arguing costs should not follow success against a licensing authority acting in good faith.
The Crown Court had treated the acquittal as strongly supporting the appeal against revocation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal by case stated against a Crown Court costs order in a firearms certificate revocation appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Crown Court costs order quashed; each party to bear own costs in the Crown Court and in the High Court appeal.
enrichment.ratio: A successful appeal against firearms certificate revocation does not ordinarily justify an adverse costs order against the Chief Constable unless there is bad faith, malice, improper motive, or Wednesbury unreasonable decision-making; later criminal acquittal on a different test does not make the revocation decision unreasonable.
legal_issues: When the Crown Court may award costs against a Chief Constable under rule 12(2)
Whether the revocation decision was unreasonable
Whether the magistrates' acquittal was relevant to the reasonableness of revocation

notes: Complete judicial review on section 72 certification; judge listed as Lord Hoffmann in metadata but judgment delivered by Sullivan J.

enrichment.short_title: Manifestly unfounded certification quashed after Secretary of State dismissed child PTSD expert evidence
key_facts: Mr Bardiqi, a Kosovan Albanian, entered the UK in February 1998 and responsibility was accepted by Germany under the Dublin Convention.
After lengthy litigation the family raised Article 8 claims based on five years' residence and the children's schooling.
Mrs Bardiqi and her son Armend had suffered severe trauma, including rape witnessed by the child; social work and psychological reports were served.
The Secretary of State certified the human rights claim as manifestly unfounded and maintained certification despite later expert evidence from Ms Saddik.
The July 2003 decision treated Ms Saddik's finding that removal would jeopardise Armend's mental health as speculative without contradicting expert evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of decisions certifying Article 8 claims as manifestly unfounded under section 72(2)(a) of the 1999 Act.
enrichment.outcome: Certification decisions in the letters of 6 March and 11 July 2003 quashed; permission to appeal refused; claimant awarded publicly funded costs.
enrichment.ratio: Section 72 certification requires that a claim be bound to fail; where an expert report credibly asserts a high risk of relapse into PTSD if a traumatised child is removed, the Secretary of State cannot lawfully dismiss that evidence as speculative and conclude Article 8(1) is not even arguably engaged.
legal_issues: Whether the section 72 manifestly unfounded threshold was satisfied
Whether the Secretary of State lawfully assessed expert evidence on Armend's mental health
How Razgar and Ullah affect Article 8 claims involving removal to a safe third country

enrichment.short_title: Costs discretion upheld where claimant lost contract claim but won smaller quantum meruit award
key_facts: Vernon-Kell claimed a 10% commission on financing arrangements for medical technology companies; the contract claim, if successful, would have exceeded £1 million.
Defendants paid £30,000 and offered a further £30,000 under Part 36; the contract claim was tried first and dismissed.
The claimant then succeeded on an amended quantum meruit claim for about £137,000 plus interest.
The deputy judge ordered the first defendant to pay the claimant's costs except for days 2 to 5 of the five-day contract trial.
No separate costs order was made against or in favour of the second defendant.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal with leave against a deputy High Court judge's costs order following split success on contract and quantum meruit claims.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; costs order upheld; appellants ordered to pay respondents' appeal costs summarily assessed at £10,647 including VAT.
enrichment.ratio: Where contract and quantum meruit claims overlap factually, a trial judge may disallow the successful party's costs for the extra trial time attributable to an unsuccessful but related contract claim without making a separate costs order in favour of the unsuccessful defendant, provided the overall costs result is within the generous discretion on costs.
legal_issues: Whether the judge erred in disallowing only days 2 to 5 of the contract trial rather than awarding defendants their contract-trial costs
How to apportion costs between split claims with substantial factual overlap
Whether the second defendant should have recovered its costs

notes: Complete Court of Appeal asylum appeal remitting internal flight issue.

enrichment.short_title: Asylum appeal allowed because tribunal failed to address internal flight in Russia

statutes_considered.title: United Nations Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees 1951

key_facts: Ms Arsanova, an ethnic Russian from Chechnya, claimed asylum in the UK in September 1997, fearing persecution linked to her husband's death and later to the Arsanov clan name.
The Secretary of State rejected the claim partly on the basis she could relocate elsewhere in Russia.
Before the special adjudicator the Home Office counsel treated internal flight as the main issue and did not contest lack of safety in Chechnya.
The adjudicator and Immigration Appeal Tribunal dismissed the appeal but did not properly determine whether relocation elsewhere in Russia would be unduly harsh.
An expert report by Robert Chenciner was admitted reluctantly but the IAT criticised it without clear contrary evidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal with full court leave against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal determination dismissing a refugee and ECHR appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on the internal flight ground; case remitted to the Immigration Appeal Tribunal for rehearing.
enrichment.ratio: Where internal flight or relocation is a live and permitted ground of appeal, the tribunal must address it specifically and explain whether relocation within the country of origin would be reasonable and not unduly harsh; failure to do so is an error of law warranting remittal.
legal_issues: Whether the IAT erred by failing to consider internal flight/relocation
Whether relocation to another part of Russia was a viable and non-harsh solution
Whether the tribunal lawfully rejected expert evidence on clan-related risk

notes: Very long quantum judgment after admitted liability; core damages figures extracted from full text.

enrichment.short_title: GNER recovered derailment damages after Railcare's admitted negligence in wheel overhaul
key_facts: Railcare negligently failed to deburr and chamfer a balance-weight hole in a Mark IV wheelset overhauled in May 1997.
A fatigue crack caused derailment of the 17:30 King's Cross to Edinburgh service on 16 June 1998 at 125 mph; liability was admitted before trial.
The trial concerned lost revenue, attributable expenses, and alleged contributory negligence for failing to detect the crack during maintenance.
GNER's net passenger revenue loss attributable to the Sandy derailment was assessed at about £1.904 million after agreed commission deductions.
Contributory negligence failed; recoverable Interfleet-related expenses were limited to £155,000 rather than the wider good-hole programme costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court Commercial Court quantum trial after admission of liability for derailment caused by negligent wheel overhaul.
enrichment.outcome: Claimant succeeded on quantum subject to deductions; no contributory negligence; judgment on damages with costs to follow.
enrichment.ratio: A tortfeasor remains liable only for losses caused by its own negligence rather than separable remedial works undertaken after derailment; lost revenue should be measured by comparing actual to best-estimate budget-based revenue with modest deductions for extraneous factors, and failure to detect an unprecedented crack is not negligent with hindsight.
legal_issues: How to quantify lost passenger and catering revenue after the derailment
Which post-derailment expenses were causally attributable to Railcare's deburring/chamfering negligence
Whether GNER was contributorily negligent in visual inspection and maintenance

notes: Complete judgment on section 21 National Assistance Act eligibility for HIV-positive asylum seekers.

enrichment.short_title: Hackney section 21 withdrawal for HIV asylum seekers upheld but senior review directed

statutes_considered.title: National Health Service and Community Care Act 1990

key_facts: Mr B and Ms H, Jamaican nationals with HIV/AIDS, received residential support under section 21 of the 1948 Act from Hackney from 2000.
After refusal of exceptional leave to remain in January 2003 they remained destitute asylum seekers appealing that decision.
In February 2003 social worker Leslie Pickering reassessed them and decided their need for care and attention no longer met section 21 criteria.
The couple and their daughters were required to leave council accommodation in March 2003 pending challenge.
Pickering did not obtain updated medical reports but visited the family; the council failed to carry out a promised senior-manager review.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of Hackney's decision withdrawing section 21 residential accommodation from destitute HIV-positive asylum seekers.
enrichment.outcome: Substantive withdrawal decisions not quashed as irrational, but order requiring review by a senior social services manager in accordance with the judgment; costs to be agreed or decided on application.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 21(1A) of the 1948 Act a destitute person subject to immigration control qualifies for residential accommodation only if illness or other circumstances make the need for care and attention more acute than destitution alone; a local authority must follow its own review policy when requested, but need not always obtain fresh medical reports if a competent social assessment visit suffices.
legal_issues: Whether the claimants' HIV-related needs satisfied section 21(1)(a) and were not solely due to destitution under section 21(1A)
Whether the assessment required up-to-date medical evidence and adequate reasons
Whether the council breached its policy by failing to conduct a senior review
